column5: Reader's preface (1997/98): British photojournalist who lived in Cape Town 1955-63 and Nairobi for ten years; reported Biafra, Mboya/Nkrumah funerals, met Nyerere, Kenyatta, Biko, Smith, Mobutu; states his subjective stance (Africa 'woefully misunderstood and misused'); the book is organised by processes (environment, ecology) rather than region and period. Popular synthesis, not primary research; treat its colonial-era and independence chapters as a secondary narrative with strong ecological emphasis

Reader's opening thesis: African population grew from ~1m (100,000 yrs ago) to ~20m by AD 200 and ~47m by AD 1500 in 'stable biological equilibrium', while out-of-Africa population reached 200m+ at AD 1 and ~300m by AD 1500, so Africa's environment (disease, soils, rainfall) limited growth. Arithmetic: 47m vs 300m means Africa was about 14 per cent of the 1500 total of the two groups (47/347). He asserts 'all the accepted markers of civilization occurred first in non-African locales -- metallurgy, agriculture, written language, the founding of cities': contested by Egyptian/Nilotic evidence (writing and cities in Egypt, Africa) and by the question of African iron-working; popular synthesis, treat as an ecology-based hypothesis not consensus. Also says stateless societies (civilised art of living in small societies without states) are a distinct African contribution. Population estimates are ESTIMATES

Roots of the settler-colonial land question (Module 5 context lesson 1): Dutch settlement at the Cape under Jan van Riebeeck landed 04/1652; Khoisan population of SW Cape ~50,000 [ESTIMATE]; labour shortage -> slaves from 1658 (Amersfoort 170 survivors of 500; Hasselt 228 of 271); Khoisan-settler war 1659 where Khoisan asked 'the natural owner or the foreign invader?' and van Riebeeck declared right of conquest; 1713 smallpox epidemic killed most Khoisan (about 9 in 10 per a contemporary source); Cape population 1793: 13,830 settlers with 14,747 slaves; frontier advanced 800 km in the 18th century; Reader links dispossession to overgrazing ecology. The apartheid land story (1913 Land Act) starts here; check Welsh's account of Cape origins and avoid claiming apartheid began in 1652 [refined]

Cape frontier violence (context for Module 5): commandos killed 503 Khoisan in 1774 and 2,480 between 1786 and 1795 per official records; captured children 'apprentices'; Xhosa-Boer first frontier war 1779-81 over Zuurveld grazing; British took the Cape 1795/1806 (confirmed 1814); Zuurveld expulsion 10/1811-03/1812 (Cradock report: 'not more Kaffir blood than necessary'); 1820 settlers (6,000) arrive. Offensive terms 'Kaffir/Hottentot' appear only as quotes; the course should use Khoisan/Xhosa and flag the historical terms. Eastern Cape wars (nine frontier wars to 1879) are the lead-in to Module 5 and to Welsh's account of the Afrikaner/British conflict [CONTEXT]

1820 British settlers (about 4,000 landed 04-06/1820, GBP 50,000 grant, 90,000 applications; only 438 of 1,004 male grantees still on the land by 05/1823; Cape wool exports ~1m lb 1842 -> 14m 1857 -> 36m 1866) and the fifth (1819) and sixth (1834-35) Frontier Wars; Governor Somerset's divide-and-rule with Ngqika. Mfecane debate: Reader reports Omer-Cooper's classic view (Shaka's Zulu expansion drove the 'scattering') and then challenges it (archaeology shows no general ecological crisis in Zululand), signalling the revisionist school (Cobbing) that attributes much of the upheaval to Delagoa Bay/slave and Cape-frontier pressures. For Module 5 treat 'Shaka caused the Mfecane' as contested and avoid it as an unqualified claim; Mfengu origin ('seekers for service') as refugees

Reader sides with the revisionist 'slaving' thesis of the Mfecane (Delagoa Bay slave trade: at least 20,000 taken c.1818-early 1830s, 1,000-6,000 males a year per Portuguese records; Dithakong 1823 'battle' reread as a massacre of up to 300 Mantatees with captives given as 'apprentices'; Ordinance 49 of 1828; Mbolompo raid 1828; Mfengu from the 1834-35 war, 17,000 captives 85 per cent women and children). He says the thesis 'is not yet proven' and 'remains contentious'. So the course must not repeat the old Shaka-as-motor story as settled and must label the revisionist reading [CONTESTED]. Relevance: origins of the 'tribal labour' and Bantustan ideology that Welsh describes; Reader notes the old story suited white-minority separatist ideology

Great Trek (Module 5 lesson 1 'roots'): Reader's account, which is revisionist about Afrikaner myth: Ordinance 50 (1828) outlawed compulsory service; emancipation from 08/1834 (four-year apprenticeship; compensation inadequate and had to be claimed in London); about 6,000 trekkers in the 1830s (~one-tenth of whites in the Cape); trekker's own words say the grievance was equality with 'Christians', not only compensation; Retief killed 06/02/1838 (Dingane's treaty text may be a forgery by Pretorius per some scholars); Weenen massacre: 41 men, 56 women, 185 children, ~250 Khoisan servants killed; Blood River 16/12/1838; Natal Republic 1839, annexed by Britain 1843 (with a non-discrimination clause); Boer republics recognised 1852 (Sand River) and 1854 (Bloemfontein). Voortrekker Monument is described as 1930s design (it was inaugurated 1949 [check]). Quote from the 1954 Verwoerd speech: 'natives must not be given the impression they will graze in the greener pastures of their masters' (Bantu Education; Act passed 1953, in force 1954 [consistent with Welsh]). Compare Welsh on Afrikaner nationalism and the Blood River covenant; use Reader only for the contested pieces

Mineral revolution as origin of the migrant-labour system (Module 5 lesson 1): diamonds 1867 near the Vaal-Harts confluence, gold 1886 south of Pretoria (Witwatersrand); Cape government borrowed over GBP 20m 1872-85; last African diamond claim holder bought out 1883; Africans' land access shrank so mine wage labour was 'little better than slave labour'. Compare Welsh on the 1913 Land Act and compounds; Reader shows the continuity from frontier labour shortage to compound labour

Kimberley diamonds (Module 5 lesson 1): first stone 1867 (21.25 carats; Eureka), Star of Africa found by Swartboy 03/1869 (83 carats), New Rush 07/1871, city named Kimberley; Cape diamond exports 16,542 carats in 1869 -> 1,080,000 carats worth over GBP 1.6m in 1872; annexation of Griqualand West 1871; 50,000 people at Kimberley within a year, ~30,000 Africans, with 50,000 migrant workers a year; 64 per cent of 1876 migrants came from over 800 km away. Reader says the compound system and pass laws of the 1880s under British rule set precedents for apartheid: this is the continuity thesis (Welsh agrees that segregation preceded 1948; check wording so course lesson 1 does not date apartheid's origins to 1948 alone) [refined]. Contains Chalmers' dismissive wording about farmers' children ('not much better than natives'), a primary-source attitude example

Origins of pass laws and compounds (Module 5 lesson 1 'before 1948'): Cape Government Notice 68 of 07/1872 (Kimberley registration depot, passes, 3-month contracts, fines/imprisonment/25 lashes, employer searches), colour-blind wording ('servants') but applied only to blacks; 1872: 1,100-1,500 departing labourers checked in December alone, of 275 without passes 250 fined and 18 flogged six lashes; locations (about 10 per cent of West Griqualand for Africans, 1876); closed/open 'compounds' from 1879 ('localization'), 22,000 Africans in seven locations by late 1880; Diamond Trade Act 1882 (presumption of guilt, no jury); De Beers Consolidated incorporated 03/1888 (Rhodes, Beit, Barnato, Stow); De Beers 1890 profit GBP 1,209,780 (52 per cent margin); British confederation drive by Carnarvon 1877-81 (Transvaal annexed 1877; wars on Xhosa 1877-8, Pedi 1877-9, Zulu 1879, Sotho from 1880; Majuba Hill 1881). Reader states 'the origins of apartheid as a legally defined policy lay here' (his interpretation). Cross-check against Welsh and the course's 1913/1936 land figures

Compounds, convicts and Wenela: closed compounds at Kimberley from 1885 (all African mineworkers by 1889), De Beers used convict labour 1884-1932; gold on the Witwatersrand 1885/86; Africans in gold mines: 15,000 (1890), 69,000 (1897), just under 190,000 (1912); Wenela/Native Labour Supply Association 1896/1900; African gold-mine wages fell from just over 15s a week (1896) to 13s (1913) while productivity rose; 1936 census: 393,000 of 1,700,000 African men aged 15-50 (23 per cent; arithmetic checked 393/1700 = 23.1%) worked in mines and allied industries. Witwatersrand produced a quarter of world gold within ten years; 29.8 per cent of world gold in 1906 [check]. Supports the lesson that the migrant-labour system predates 1948 by 60 years; the 1913 Land Act and 1936 Trust and Land Act (Welsh) are the legal land frame

POPULATION-BASE DISCREPANCY for the Congo death-toll table: Reader says the Congo Free State (2.5 million sq km, recognised 05/1885) had 'a population of about 10 million people'; Hochschild says 'some twenty million Africans' and builds the ~10 million loss on a halving from about 20m to the 10m counted in 1924 (via the 1919 commission, Liebrechts and Vansina). If the 1885 base were only 10m, 'reduced by half' would give about 5 million lost, not 10 million. So the toll depends entirely on the unknown pre-1885 population and on the 'half' premise; label [ESTIMATE/CONTESTED] and give the range, with the base figure stated. Also arithmetic: Hochschild's '76 times Belgium' implies about 2.3 million sq km (76 x 30,500), close to Reader's 2.5 million; use 'about 2.3-2.5 million sq km'. Other points: Leopold's 1876 Geographical Conference (International African Association; Britain declined to join); 'the Zanzibar flag' used by Stanley; Stanley's 999-day crossing killed 3 Europeans and 173 Africans (Reader); Cameron proclaimed a British protectorate over the Congo basin 28/12/1874 but Britain repudiated it

Berlin Conference facts, checked against Hochschild and Moyo: opened 15/11/1884 (all agree); Reader says Berlin Act signed 25/02/1885 (the General Act is usually dated 26/02/1885 [check]); Reader says 'thirteen nations attended' but lists thirteen names that omit France and Germany, so with them it is the standard fourteen participating states (Moyo says fourteen); Free State proclaimed by royal decree 05/1885 (Hochschild: 29/05/1885), inhabitants told a month later; Germany recognised the IAC 08/11/1884; US Senate resolution 11/04/1884 and executive recognition 22/04/1884 (Hochschild) describe different steps; France's pre-emption (right of first refusal) in exchange for recognition; Britain's 'tacit acceptance' of Leopold's frontiers by a clerk's blunder in 1885. Reader, like Hochschild, lets the IAC be 'trapped between France and Portugal': Berlin recognised an existing claim rather than partitioning Africa (the course should say 'set ground rules and recognised Leopold's Congo')

Reader's death-toll sentence conflicts with Hochschild and with his own earlier line: 'Prior to the arrival of the concessionaires the Congo population was estimated at least 20 million. An official census taken in 1911 revealed only 8.5 million left.' (a) Reader earlier (same chapter) gave the 1885 population as 'about 10 million'; (b) Hochschild says no territory-wide census existed until the 1920s (first reckoning 1924, about 10 million): a '1911 census' of 8.5m is not supported there; the 1911 figure is a Belgian administrative estimate, not a census [check]. So Reader's 20m-to-8.5m (a loss of 11.5m) is a third version beside Hochschild's ~10m and Ndaywel's 13m->10m. Use the range, name each source and basis (administrative estimate vs reconstruction), keep [ESTIMATE/CONTESTED]

Further Reader slips to avoid: (1) 'Conrad captained a trading steamer on the Congo in 1890 and 1891' (Hochschild: Conrad spent about six months in 1890, was an apprentice officer and did not gain command; he left after a quarrel and illness); (2) 'Casement, British Consul to the Free State for eleven years' (Hochschild: Casement lived in the Congo 1880s, became consul in 1900; the investigation was 1903); (3) rubber export series printed as '1,300 tonnes by 1896, to 1,300 tonnes by 1898' (duplicate figure, probably a misprint) ahead of 6,000 tonnes in 1901 and 100 tonnes in 1890; (4) Leopold's 1908 compensation given as GBP 2m (Hochschild: 50m francs plus 45.5m for his projects, 110m of debts assumed: a different sum, not comparable); (5) ABIR quota given as four kilos per fortnight (matches Hochschild 3-4 kg), 47,000 gatherers in 1906 (matches), ABIR concession exhausted of rubber by 1906. Confirmations: Fondation de la Couronne 250,000 sq km; pneumatic tyre dates (Dunlop 1888, Michelin 1891); Nsala photograph

African agency in the Scramble (Module 1 'forms of rule/treaties'): Lewanika (Lozi Litunga, Barotseland, western Zambia) actively sought British protection and ceded 'rights over 200,000 square miles' in exchange for promised education and payments of GBP 2,000 a year that he said never arrived [see rest of chapter for the Lochner/Rhodes concession and the 1900 agreement]; invited to Edward VII's coronation (1902). Reader's framing: treaties drawn through translators; terms like perpetual land rights 'had no direct counterpart in African understanding'. Also his account of Lozi society includes slavery, human sacrifice and witch trials (from missionary Arnot); a cautionary note for balance: use Lozi as an example of an African state with its own empire, a conqueror and slaveholder that sought alliance for its own ends. Reader repeats 'Berlin Conference at which Africa was carved out' (chapter blurb) which Hochschild disputes: wording to avoid

Lochner Concession as the treaty-fraud worked example (Module 1 forms of rule; beats the generic example): Rhodes bought the Ware mining concession (28/06/1889, Ware paid for with GBP 200 a year and 4 per cent royalty; resold for GBP 500 then GBP 9,000 + 10,000 BSAC shares); agent Frank Lochner (arrived 04/1890) misrepresented the British South Africa Company as an arm of the Queen's government; Lewanika signed 26/06/1890: GBP 2,000 a year, schools, telegraph, a British Resident, in exchange for exclusive perpetual trade, mining and construction rights (200,000+ sq miles). Company paid nothing for seven years (arrears 7 x 2,000 = GBP 14,000, checked), then GBP 850 a year without back-pay; Resident arrived 1897; Colonial Office conceded Lochner 'made too free use of Her Majesty's name' but the agreement stood; Lewanika's title 'King' abolished 10/1907, Barotseland a province of Northern Rhodesia 1911; hut tax from 1902 to push men into mine labour. Britain finally took over from BSAC in 1924. Lewanika attended Edward VII's coronation (1902), the 'admiral's uniform' is a myth (a surplus ambassador's uniform per Reader). Link Zambia (Moyo, Module 6) back to this history

Colonial boundaries (Module 1 and Module 4/7 inheritance): 177 ethnic 'culture areas' divided by borders (Reader's cite: a boundary survey; Burkina Faso's borders cut 21, Nigeria-Cameroon 14); at his writing (c.1997) Africa had 46 states plus five island states and >46,000 km of land boundaries (now 54 AU member states after Eritrea 1993, South Sudan 2011 etc. [check current]); 15 landlocked states 'more than the rest of the world put together' (c.1997; current count 16 [check]); Anglo-German 1900 Kenya-Tanzania boundary still described by baobab trees; Benin-Nigeria border 53 per cent unsurveyed; railways rarely cross frontiers (East African railway reached Uganda 1901, cutting cotton freight from GBP 200 to GBP 2.40 per tonne). Economic reality: Africa ~5 per cent of Britain's trade in the 1870s; BSAC paid no dividend in 33 years; Pope-Hennessy 1890 'Is Central Africa Worth Having?'. Effective occupation (Berlin Act) forced the pace of the Scramble: Reader's own framing supports 'Berlin set the rules; borders came by bilateral deals'

Date slip: Reader writes that Bismarck told the Zanzibar consul in 'October 1899' he had had enough of colonies and 'a few months later' resigned; Bismarck resigned in 03/1890, so the date should be 10/1889 [check]. The Bismarck colonial turn was 05-1884 (Togo, Cameroon flags 07/1884; Angra Pequena 08/1884; East Africa 02/1885): correct per standard accounts. Avoid copying the 1899 figure

Reader's upbeat paragraph on German colonial rule ('a miniature Wirtschaftswunder', 1914 Reichstag welfare resolutions 'far more comprehensive than any other') sits beside, and is not reconciled with, the genocide of the Herero and Nama (1904-08) and the Maji Maji war (1905-07) in the same empire; the course's Module 2 lessons must keep the violence in view; treat the 1914 resolutions as intentions never implemented (Reader says so). Also Hochschild's point that Herero genocide got little protest in Britain

Adwa and Ethiopia (Module 1 lesson on resistance/Adwa; checks the course's figures): Reader gives the battle on 01/03/1896 with Italian losses 3,179 officers and men killed plus ~2,000 locally recruited troops (over 40 per cent of their fighting force) and 11,000 rifles lost; Ethiopian casualties ~7,000 dead and 10,000 wounded; Menelik's force ~100,000 mobilised from 09/1895; peace treaty 10/1896 (Addis Ababa) recognised Ethiopian independence; Eritrea stayed Italian; Massawa seized 1885; Menelik's 1891 circular to the European powers; Italian/Amharic text difference in the Wuchale treaty (Article 17). Compare with Module 1 Adwa numbers and Moyo's 'Adowa 1896'. Also resistance quotes (Machemba 1890, Witbooi 1894, Prempeh 1891, Wobogo 1895, Makombe 1895)

Reader's balanced thesis on conquest (useful corrective to a pure 'resistance' narrative): the 'thin white line' was thin (Nyasaland 1891 with GBP 10,000 a year, ten civilians, two officers, 70 Sikhs, 85 porters; Northern Nigeria 2,000 soldiers + 6 administrators for 10m people), colonial rule depended on African collaboration; but technology (quinine cut malaria deaths by about four-fifths, breech-loaders 1866, repeaters 1885, Maxim gun 1884; Omdurman: British killed at least 10,800 Sudanese with 49 own dead; 1890 Brussels Convention banned arms sales to Africans) made the outcome 'inevitable'; he also claims resistance involved fewer than half of 1 per cent of Africa's ~129m people (645,000) and 'any attempt to characterise the early colonial period in terms of conquest and resistance is seriously misleading' -- a deliberately provocative claim that most African historians dispute; present as one view. Population: 47m (1500) -> 129m (1900) [ESTIMATES]; 1885-1914 drought turn (wet 1870-95 then dry 1895-1920) and jiggers, smallpox, rinderpest as 'ecological' explanations for weak resistance

Rinderpest (ecological context for conquest, new lesson material for Module 1 beyond arms): introduced with cattle imported by Italian forces at Massawa 1889; killed 90-95 per cent of Africa's cattle by the early 1900s, 5.5m cattle south of the Zambezi, 2.5m south of the 1,600 km South African fence (over GBP 1m spent); Baumann estimated two-thirds of the Maasai died; Lugard said it 'favoured our enterprise'; wild ungulates also died, tsetse fly then spread through regrown bush, sleeping sickness killed 200,000 in southern Uganda by 1906 (about two in three of those surviving the previous decade), and many present game parks (Serengeti, Tsavo, Selous, Kruger etc.) are in former cattle country. Reader's ecological-historiography claim that these parks were once farmed/herded is contested; present as Reader's argument and note that rinderpest, drought and disease are sourced to Kjekshus-type ecological history [CONTESTED]. Links to Hochschild's point that disease (sleeping sickness) was worsened by trauma and malnutrition and that Leopold's apologists blame it

Herero and Nama (Module 2, checks the course): rising 12/01/1904 (about 100+ German men killed, women and children spared); Trotha arrived 06/1904 with the Kaiser's order, Vernichtungsbefehl proclamation (10/1904, Reader says withdrawn two months later on Berlin's orders); 24,000 Herero trapped at the desert edge, 5,000 escaped to Bechuanaland/Cape; Witbooi (aged ~80, a Nama leader) rose and was mortally wounded 10/1905; 17,000 German troops and GBP 20m cost; camps (by 1907 over half of the 15,000 Herero and 2,000 Nama prisoners dead); 1911 census: Herero 15,000 of ~80,000, Nama 9,800 of 20,000. ARITHMETIC CHECK: (80,000+20,000) -> (15,000+9,800) = 24,800 left = 24.8 per cent, so 75.2 per cent of the combined population died, matching Reader's '75 per cent'; Herero alone lost 81 per cent, Nama 51 per cent. Note Hochschild gives Herero 80,000 (1903) -> under 20,000 (1906); consistent. Settlers 2,000 (1896) -> 4,700 (1903)

Maji Maji (Module 2): trigger 07/1905 at Nandete in the Matumbi Hills, uprooting cotton on the compulsory communal plots (4,000 ha; ~160,000 men obliged; pay 35 cents for the first year, none after); prophet Kinjikitile Ngwale (spirit Hongo/Bokero, maji medicine said to turn bullets to water), captured and hanged early; failed attack at Mahenge 30/08/1905 where Reader says machine guns destroyed the columns; over twenty ethnic groups joined; Governor von Goetzen chose famine: scorched earth; last leaders hanged 18/07/1908; deaths: official German 75,000 vs 250,000-300,000 by 1960s oral evidence (perhaps a third of the population), most from starvation; rebels killed 15 Europeans and 389 Africans attached to German forces. Selous game reserve carved from depopulated land; tsetse spread. Reader notes the bullet-to-water belief; Hochschild records the same belief among the Kuba in 1908: add cross-reference. Range 75,000 to 300,000 must carry [ESTIMATE/CONTESTED]

Anglo-Boer War (Module 5 lesson 1): 10/1899-31/05/1902; Britain mobilised 448,000, 22,000 died (13,250 from disease), cost GBP 222m; Boers 88,000 mobilised, 7,000+ dead; camps: 111,619 in camps by 10/1901, 27,927 Boer deaths 06/1901-05/1902 (about 10 per cent of the two republics' Boer population; 22,000+ children under 16, 4,000+ adult women); black Africans: at least 115,700 sent to camps, 14,154 died (so about 12 per cent died; arithmetic 14,154/115,700 = 12.2%); 100,000+ Africans served as scouts, guards and servants, 10,000-30,000 as armed combatants; 6,000 km of barbed wire, 8,000 blockhouses. Welsh and Reader agree war fostered Afrikaner nationalism (course: avoid describing the war as only white-on-white). Reader also notes the Jameson Raid 1895 and gold as the cause (economic interpretation)

Treaty of Vereeniging 31/05/1902 clause eight postponed any decision on African voting rights until self-government returned to the former republics (effectively indefinitely); post-war: only GBP 1 in every GBP 4 assessed as war compensation to Africans in the Transvaal was paid; discriminatory laws retained; mining wages cut. Strong support for Module 5 lesson 1 (why 1910 Union excluded Africans) and a document to cite. Africans' hopes of British victory dashed (Louis Botha run off his own farm by African tenants). Also check the course's 1910 Union of South Africa Act wording against Welsh

First World War in Africa (Module 2 context and Module 3 Pan-Africanism): first shots fired in the Anglo-French invasion of Togo, German surrender 26/08/1914; SW Africa captured by South Africa 1915; Cameroon early 1916; Lettow-Vorbeck surrendered three days after the armistice (kept ~160,000 allied troops engaged with never more than 15,000); over 1 million African troops and 1 million+ carriers in East Africa alone (>100,000 deaths there), 2.5 million Africans in war work (~2 per cent of the population), 200,000+ African deaths; French colonies sent 450,000 soldiers to Europe (50,000 from Algeria); French West Africa recruited 50,000 more in 1915-16 ('a new slave trade'); Congo impressed up to 260,000 porters; British refused African troops against Germans in Europe. Hochschild gives the Congo's WWI forced labour too (1359 of 83,518 men died in one district). Estimates; sources inconsistent on totals [ESTIMATE]

'Invention of tradition' thesis for Module 7 Rwanda and Module 6 Biafra (constructivist view): Reader argues colonial codification of customary law, 'tribal' units and chiefs created fixed ethnic identities ('Europeans believed Africans belonged to tribes; Africans built tribes to belong to'; Zulu as a discrete ethnic group only from the 1870s; Kikuyu-Maasai enmity a colonial fiction; Zambian chief: 'we were not Soli until 1937'). He also says pan-Hausa/Igbo/Yoruba identities pre-dated colonial rule but were not static. For Rwanda: German ethnographers described Twa, Hutu and Tutsi with a 'Hamitic' origin story for the Tutsi (a discredited racial hypothesis; the course should name it as colonial theory, not fact); Tutsi about 12-15 per cent of the population, Hutu ~85 per cent; Germans chose exclusively Tutsi chiefs; Rwanda 312 and Burundi 233 persons per sq km in 1993. Specialists (Newbury, Mamdani, Prunier) agree colonial rule hardened identities but argue Tutsi-Hutu categories pre-existed in some form [CONTESTED/refined]; present both

Interwar colonial states (Module 1/2): Africa's population 120m (1880) -> 165m (1935), +37.5 per cent (arithmetic 165/120 = 1.375, checked), 'despite a net loss during the early colonial period'; tropical Africa under 2 per cent of Britain's 1913 trade and under 1 per cent of France's, Belgian Congo 1 per cent of Belgian trade (1912), German colonies under 1 per cent (1910): colonies were not obviously profitable for the metropoles (cf. Rodney's argument that they were the source of capital; the two readings should be shown side by side); League of Nations mandates 'sacred trust of civilisation'; District Commissioners (Lumley memoir, Tanganyika 1923-45); government anthropologists (Rattray, Meek, Talbot); 'peace' of the 1920s because of fixed borders (Reader's claim that most African wars since independence have been within borders -- partly contradicted by the 1998-2003 Congo war and Eritrea-Ethiopia [dated])

Rwanda ID cards (Module 7 Rwanda lesson 1): Reader says Belgian authorities introduced an identity card specifying 'tribe' in 1926 and applied a '10 cows or more = Tutsi, fewer = Hutu' rule. Most Rwanda historians date the compulsory ethnic identity cards to 1933-35 (census of 1933-34, cards from 1935) while the 1926 date is associated with the Belgian administrative reform that removed Hutu chiefs; the ten-cow rule is widely repeated but is a simplification of an inconsistent practice [CONTESTED, check Prunier/Mamdani/Newbury]. Do NOT teach '1926 cards' as settled; use 'in the 1930s Belgium made ethnic identity a legal category on identity cards'. Also: Belgium got Ruanda-Urundi as a League mandate (it had hoped to swap it to Portugal for the south bank of the Congo, 1919); forced unpaid labour 29 days a year; coffee introduced 1925 (50 tonnes 1929 -> 2,000 tonnes 1937); more than 2 per cent of able-bodied Rwandan men worked in Congo mines in 1930. Reader's interpretation that Belgium's rule turned the Tutsi-Hutu relation into master-servant ('essentially no more than') is the standard colonial-hardening argument. Also 1931 Belgian missionary concluding they shared a common culture

Emergent elite and ethnicity at independence (Module 4, links to Module 6 Biafra/Module 7): 1938 only ~11,000 Africans in secondary school in all sub-Saharan Africa (population >165m); William Ponty graduated 1,500 Africans 1918-39; Fort Hare averaged under 4 graduates a year 1923-36; Achimota 37 London-degree students 1938; perhaps 12 black French West Africans with degrees 1905-40 (Senghor among them); Lincoln University (Azikiwe 1931, Nkrumah 1939). Compare Rodney's 16 Congo graduates at independence. Population 142m (1920) -> 200m (late 1940s) -> ~300m (1960s); urban share 18.4 per cent in 1960 (UN); Congo-Brazzaville >30, Ghana 23.3, Zaire 22.3, Nigeria 13.1, Kenya 7.4, Rwanda 2.4, Burundi 2.2 per cent. Reader's 'Robin Hood' politics and the quote 'whenever ethnicity confronted class-consciousness ethnicity has almost invariably triumphed' (Odinga's Luo base; Awolowo's Yoruba base) explain why parties split along ethnic lines after independence [a generalisation, labelled so]

Rwanda education and the colonial state (Module 7): Church took over schooling under the 1930s 'Contrat Scolaire' (about 47 francs per pupil, 600 francs per qualified teacher per class of 25) negotiated by Bishop Leon Classe; Classe told missionaries 'you must choose the Tutsi' because posts 'will be reserved henceforth for young Tutsi' (Reader's quote of the colonial policy); German ethnographer Hans Meyer's praise of Tutsi 'proud reserve'. So the favoured-minority structure was built by schooling and chieftaincy decisions, setting up the 1959 'social revolution' and later violence. Cross-check with the course's Module 7 first lesson and Prunier/Mamdani; Reader writes that 'no such hopes existed for Rwanda and Burundi'

Road to 1959 in Rwanda (Module 7 lesson 1 'roots'): Hutu Manifesto 03/1957 (critique of 'the political monopoly of one race, the Tutsi race'); first Rwandan university-educated person Anastase Makuza (Hutu, Kisantu 1955) could not get a job; Catholic seminaries were virtually the only higher-education route for Hutu until 1956; Vice-Governor-General Harroy in 12/1958 proposed dropping the labels Hutu/Tutsi from official use and Hutu rejected it as 'Tutsi obfuscation'; Classe's 'racial aristocracy'. Reader's account is the colonial-structure explanation; note it describes a 1957 Manifesto where the Hutu leaders already used a racialised vocabulary, a detail which historians (Prunier, Mamdani) debate. Safe-to-teach points: colonial favouring of Tutsi in schooling and posts, Hutu elite emerging in the 1950s

Pan-African Congress numbering: Reader calls Manchester 10/1945 'the sixth Pan-African Congress'; it is conventionally the FIFTH (Paris 1919 second, London/Brussels/Paris 1921 second session, London 1923 third, New York 1927 fourth, Manchester 1945 fifth). Check which number the course uses and keep 'fifth' for Manchester. Reader's account is otherwise useful: mostly African delegates (Nkrumah, Kenyatta), resolutions 'We are determined to be free... autonomy and independence'. Also Rodney's Brazzaville date 1948 vs Reader's 'early 1944' (Reader correct); Atlantic Charter (08/1941) clause three and Churchill's Commons gloss that it applied only to Nazi-occupied Europe

Reader's sentence on South Africa's franchise is wrong or compressed and conflicts with Welsh: he says Malan's Nationalists 'within months' of 1948 packed the Senate and removed the entrenched clause so 'henceforth only whites could vote'. Africans in the Cape were removed from the common roll in 1936 (Hertzog's Representation of Natives Act), well before 1948, and the Coloured vote was removed through the Separate Representation of Voters Act contest and the 1955 Senate enlargement (effective 1956), not within months [check against Welsh dates before editing the course]. Safe facts: Union of South Africa 31/05/1910 (Louis Botha PM, eight years to the day after Vereeniging); national convention Durban 10/1908, thirty white delegates (12 Cape, 8 Transvaal, 5 OFS, 5 Natal; 14 Afrikaners, 16 British origin); Cape franchise qualification (literacy + GBP 50 income or GBP 75 property), 1909 registered voters 85 per cent white, 10 per cent Coloured, 5 per cent African; two-thirds clause entrenching it; population 1910: 4m Africans, 500,000 Coloured, 150,000 Indian, 1.275m whites (so Africans = 4/(4+0.5+0.15+1.275)=67.5% of 5.925m)

Mau Mau (Module 2 lesson): Reader's figures: emergency declared 10/1952; ~2,000 loyalist Kikuyu killed; official rebel death toll 11,500; 32 white civilians killed ('fewer than Nairobi road deaths'); Britain deployed eleven infantry battalions and a heavy-bomber squadron plus 21,000 police and a 25,000-strong Home Guard; Kenyatta tried, 7 years' hard labour, released 1961. His framing (violence mainly Kikuyu against Kikuyu loyalists; no mention of the detention camps, forced villagisation or torture) is the older colonial-flavoured account and omits what Anderson and Elkins documented (tens of thousands detained; deaths in the camps; rebel deaths estimated higher than the official 11,500: Anderson ~20,000+, Elkins far higher and contested [CONTESTED]). The course must use ranges with a source and say the 11,500 is the official British count. Kenyatta slip: Reader says he was 'installed as President of independent Kenya in 1963'; he became Prime Minister at self-government/independence (12/12/1963) and the republic's first President in 12/1964 [check]. Also Reader's 'Belgian Congo no demands for independence' (contrast Hochschild/Rodney: 1959 Leopoldville riots)

Congo to independence (Module 4 lesson and cross-check for Hochschild's afterword): Van Bilsen's Thirty-Year Plan 1956 ('an ineluctable evolution'); 04/01/1959 Leopoldville riots (49 dead, 241 wounded official; unofficial >200 dead); 13/01/1959 announcement and Baudouin's pledge of independence; Brussels round table 01-02/1960, independence date fixed 27/01/1960 for 30/06/1960 (a Thursday, checked); 53 then 120 parties; elections 05/1960 MNC 33 of 137 seats; Lumumba (b.1925) PM, Kasavubu president. Capacity at independence: only 3 Congolese in the top three civil-service grades vs 4,872 Belgians (3+4,872 = 4,875 posts; Hochschild: 3 of about 5,000, consistent), 136 children completed full secondary education in 1959, no Congolese doctors, lawyers or army officers (Rodney: 16 graduates; Hochschild: fewer than thirty graduates; use a range 'a few dozen at most' with definitions); black-to-white wage ratio 1 to 40 (1955); 10 per cent of the population at school 1955; first Congolese bishop 1956. Force Publique mutiny 05-06/07/1960: 25,000 men, 1,100 Belgian officers; Mobutu (clerk, ex-journalist, Lumumba's secretary) made chief of staff; 25,000 Belgians fled; Katanga secession 11/07/1960 (Tshombe, Conakat); UN troops: 3,500 first, up to 19,000 from 26 countries; Lumumba's 30/06 reply to Baudouin

Lumumba's fall and death, compared with Hochschild (Module 4/6/7 Congo): Reader: Soviet aid from 08/1960 (15 Ilyushins, 300+ technicians, requested 15/08); US ambassador's 19/07/1960 cable ('destroy Lumumba government'); NSC 18/08/1960; Dulles read Eisenhower's remarks as 'implicit authorization'; toothbrush poison and sniper-rifle plans abandoned; Kasavubu dismissed Lumumba 05/09/1960; Mobutu first coup 14/09/1960 (Lumumba in office 76 days: arithmetic 30/06 to 14/09 = 31+31+14 = 76, checked); Lumumba arrested end of 11/1960, flown to Katanga 17/01/1961 and killed by Katangese officials and Belgian mercenaries. Hochschild (Church Committee, Kelly, De Witte): NSC subcommittee authorised the assassination, Belgian pilot and officer, body dissolved in acid, Belgian government apology 2001. Reader is weaker on US authorisation ('implicit') and on Belgian role; present as: US officials planned his murder, Belgian and Katangese forces carried out the killing, Belgium apologised in 2001. Mobutu: second coup 10/1965 (Reader), 'Zaire' renaming: Reader dates the authenticity campaign three years after the 1967 constitution (about 1970); Hochschild says Zaire was named in 1971 [check; usually 1971 for country, 1972 for his own name]

Nigeria to Biafra (Module 6 Biafra lesson; compare Rodney): Reader's sequence: 15/01/1966 majors' coup (Balewa, Akintola, the Sardauna of Sokoto killed; Ironsi takes power; 6 of 7 conspirators Igbo; no Igbo politician killed), Ironsi's May unitary decree abolishing the regions -> northern riots (several hundred Igbo killed); counter-coup end 07/1966 (Ironsi killed; Gowon leader); further northern pogroms (thousands killed, more than 1 million refugees to the East by end of 1966); Ojukwu declares Biafra 30/05/1967; war from 07/1967; surrender 01/1970 after thirty months; reconciliation ('no reparations', amnesty). This confirms that the 1966 anti-Igbo pogroms are well documented, so Rodney's 'ethnic war is a myth' claim must be limited to pre-colonial times. Post-war: states multiplied (12 in 1967, 19 in 1976, 21, 30 then 36), oil revenue up 34 times 1968-77, Dutch disease (Nigerian per-head GDP growth 1.7 per cent in 1970s, 1.1 per cent in 1980s), population 42m (independence) -> 92m, per-head income US$310 (1993); Abiola election annulled 1993. Reader counts the war's death toll nowhere here (check the course's Biafra deaths range separately: 1-3 million is commonly cited, mostly starvation [ESTIMATE])

Independence overview: UN resolution 12/1960 that unpreparedness is no pretext; 16 independences in 1960, 38 by 1965, 45 by 1975; Reader: more than 70 coups in 32 countries between Olympio's assassination (13/01/1963 Togo; 'black Africa's first coup', Eyadema) and Mobutu's fall 1997; only 5 of the OAU founders (Cameroon, Ivory Coast, Senegal, Tanzania, Tunisia) had no violent change of government by 1997; OAU founded 05/1963 at Addis Ababa by 30 (Reader) states pledging to keep colonial borders; Nyerere's 'nonsensical boundaries' but must stay; sub-Saharan GDP per head grew 1.5 per cent a year 1965-80 (World Bank 1992) vs India 1.3; Ghana income per head GBP 70, Nigeria GBP 29, India GBP 25 (1960); by 1989 only 7 of 45 sub-Saharan states kept vestiges of democracy, only Botswana held competitive elections regularly; Dahomey/Benin six coups in ten years. Dated ('more than 70 coups' count), check current coup database [check current]

Rwanda 1959-62 (Module 7 lesson 1): Reader: Belgium switched sides to the Hutu in the late 1950s; Tutsi chiefs dismissed from early 1960, about 130,000 Tutsi fled to the Congo, Burundi, Tanzania and Uganda; communal elections 07/1960: Parmehutu won 210 of 229 communes; Gitarama 28/01/1961 'legal coup' declared the republic before 25,000 people; UN-supervised legislative elections 09/1961; formal independence 01/07/1962 with Kayibanda as president; Tutsi 9 per cent of the population officially; ethnic quotas of 9 per cent in schools and jobs. (Hochschild/Reader differ in detail from other accounts, e.g. 1959 Toussaint violence is not named here.) Reader's note that Rwandan nationalism was 'inspired by ambitions to take over an oppressive indigenous hegemony which the colonial authorities installed'. Verify dates against a specialist (Prunier) before course edits

Rwanda genocide figures and chain (Module 7): Reader: Inyenzi attacks from 1960; after the 23/12/1963 Inyenzi raid from Burundi Hutu gangs killed an estimated 10,000 Tutsi and the government executed ~20 prominent Tutsi; Habyarimana's coup 05/07/1973; RPF invasion 10/1990 (army 5,000 -> 24,000 -> 35,000+ in 1993; arms from Egypt $6m 1992 with French facilitation, South Africa $5.9m, US $600,000 in 1993); International Commission: ~2,000 killed 10/1990-01/1993, 'privatising' violence via militia; Arusha Accords 08/1993 (RPF 40 per cent of troops, 50 per cent of high command); Radio Rwanda and independent radio incitement; plane shot down 06/04/1994 (Reader: cause 'never fully explained', circumstantial evidence points at extremists -- contested, check); genocide 100 days. Toll: UN 'definitive' 500,000 (he says possibly conservative); his own census-subtraction estimate 800,000-850,000 Tutsi plus 10,000-30,000 Hutu, Tutsi population ~930,000 -> no more than ~130,000. ARITHMETIC CHECK: 930,000-130,000 = 800,000 dead = 86 per cent of the Tutsi; per survivor 800/130 = 6.2 (850/130 = 6.5), so his 'for every Tutsi remaining alive seven had died' is rounded up (about six). 800,000/ ~7.3m population = ~11 per cent (Reader: 'more than 10 per cent'). 60,000 bodies buried in Kigali, ~40,000 bodies floated into Uganda; militia ~50,000; presidential guard 1,500. Range for course: about 500,000 to 800,000+ [ESTIMATE/CONTESTED]; RPF took Gisenyi 18/07/1994; >1m fled into Zaire in a week

Why apartheid ended -- a rival thesis to Welsh (Module 5 lesson 4): Reader argues it ended because it became unaffordable and demographically unsustainable: population tripled 12.671m (1951) -> 38.9m (1991) (arithmetic 38.9/12.671 = 3.07x, checked); whites fell from 21 per cent (1951) to 14 per cent (1985) toward 9 per cent by 2010 while blacks rose from 68 to 76 per cent; GDP per head fell 1.1 per cent 1980-87; three parliamentary chambers and ten departments of education/health/welfare; sanctions and disinvestment 'increased the load'; verdict: 'nothing ideological about the relinquishing of power... apartheid was no longer affordable'; unemployment ~20 per cent in 1994, need 3.5 per cent growth to hold unemployment steady and 7.5 per cent to reduce it. Welsh stresses deadlock/hurting stalemate, erosion of Afrikaner resolve and the debt standstill (07/1985); present the demographic-economic reading as one of at least two schools, not the answer [CONTESTED]. Slip: Reader says Mandela was 'gaoled for treason in 1964' (the 1964 Rivonia verdict was sabotage and related charges; Welsh has the 1962 arrest and 27 years served) -- do not repeat. 1994 election 26-29/04/1994 (he gives 26/04)

Reader closes with Mandela's 27 years of incarceration (matches Welsh: arrested 05/08/1962, released 11/02/1990, i.e. 27 years 6 months) and the 1994 election as the high point; Soyinka's 'Rwanda is our nightmare, South Africa is our dream' (05/1994). The pairing of Rwanda and South Africa as extremes is Reader's device, useful as a closing discussion question across Modules 5 and 7
